project_name: BioValue AI demo: fictional softwood kraft lignin stream
disclaimers: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.
BioValue AI gives indicative decision support. It does not guarantee profitability, does not verify customer demand, and does not constitute engineering approval.

Gross margin, profitability, NPV, and IRR are not calculated. They need capital costs, fixed costs, a discount rate, a time horizon, and agreed definitions, none of which are available yet. Gross contribution excludes capital costs, fixed costs, and the value of the feedstock in its current use.
Scores use a 1-5 scale. A criterion that was not assessed lowers data completeness; it is never counted as a low score.

constraints: Lignin is currently used as internal boiler fuel, so diverting it to another use would require changing that current use.
No lignin dryer is available; buyers requiring dry powder would need drying equipment or a drying service.
Fractionation and chemical-modification equipment are not available at the mill.
The stream leaves as moist filter cake, which constrains handling and increases the mass shipped compared with dry product.
Molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, and sodium content are missing, limiting pathway qualification and ash-related assessment.
data_quality_notes: The record is explicitly fictional demo data: the mill and stream are invented, and all values are illustrative assumptions rather than measurements.
The reported moisture is uncertain, and the lignin-content method is only stated for illustration; both should be verified with mill-specific measurements and documented analytical methods.
Other reported composition values and variability ranges are also assumptions; do not use them to make commercial or technical decisions without replacing them with mill data.
agent.summary: Validated fictional softwood kraft lignin filter-cake profile. The recorded dry-matter balance and composition check passed, and each of the three missing measured properties has a corresponding data-gap entry; the profile is not evidence about an actual mill.

carbohydrates_pct.method: Total sugars after acid hydrolysis (stated for illustration)

data_gaps.next_step: Replace the profile with the mill's own lab data and production records.

data_gaps.next_step: Request an inorganic element analysis of the ash.

supported_claims.EV-PF-01#1: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#4: Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#2: UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#R1: Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#3: UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
supported_claims.EV-PF-04#2: With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin can partially replace phenol in phenol-formaldehyde resin, which is used for adhesives in plywood and other wood-based panels.
Lignin-phenol-formaldehyde resin is documented for veneer plywood, with a supplier reporting industrial proof and bonding performance meeting EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3.

target_customers.statement: Plywood and wood-based-panel adhesive producers are the clearest implied customer types for lignin-based PF resin.

competing_materials.statement: Phenol in conventional phenol-formaldehyde resin is the incumbent material that lignin can partially replace.

qualification_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin needs activation or depolymerization before use in PF resin.
A supplier reports its LPF resin meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood; it also reports formaldehyde-emission test results under EN 717-2.
A laboratory study reports that resin containing depolymerized lignin met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in that study.

limitations: The UPM performance and cost information is vendor literature without a cited test report; its lignin is not identified as kraft lignin.
The reported replacement levels summarize studies or supplier claims rather than results from one commercial plant.
The laboratory study used poplar plywood, and its Chinese standard is named inconsistently in the paper.
The supplied feedstock profile is fictional and lacks measured molecular weight and phenolic hydroxyl content; it also reports no mill dryer or modification equipment.
missing_information: The evidence does not establish current lignin prices, market volumes for lignin-based PF resin, named buyers, contract terms, or regional demand.
It does not establish whether this fictional moist filter-cake stream can meet a buyer's specifications or the costs of drying and required pretreatment.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence includes a supplier claim of industrially proven LPF resin and documented plywood performance, but it does not document commercial sales to named buyers. This supports industry-level validation rather than the rubric's commercial-sales level.

supported_claims.EV-PU-01#1: Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#1: Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#3: Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#1: The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#2: In cited studies, kraft lignin replaced up to about 20% of polyol after oxypropylation, up to 50% when depolymerized and oxypropylated, and up to 100% when liquefied in a bio-based polyol.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#2: Two of the three foams that failed were made with kraft lignin; they failed the compressive strength and/or closed-cell content requirements.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#R1: Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#R1: Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
supported_claims.EV-PU-05#1: Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.

applications.statement: Lignin is studied as a partial replacement for petroleum-based polyol in rigid PUR/PIR foam.

Unmodified lignin has also been tested as a partial polyol replacement in flexible polyurethane foam; the study suggests kraft-lignin foams may suit heavy-duty uses because they were denser and stiffer.
A review describes kraft lignin use in polyurethane foams, panels, coatings, and rubber replacement, while noting that reported substitution levels depend on lignin treatment.

target_customers.statement: Rigid and flexible polyurethane foam producers are implied as potential customer types by the foam formulations studied.

competing_materials.statement: Petroleum-based polyols are the incumbent material partially replaced by lignin in the documented polyurethane studies.

qualification_requirements.statement: One rigid-foam study reports that foams with lignin passed measured ASTM C1029-15 Type 1 specifications, while two of the three failed samples were made with kraft lignin and failed compressive-strength and/or closed-cell requirements.
For rigid polyurethane foam, the evidence cites a total hydroxyl value above 200 mg KOH/g as an acceptable range; this is total hydroxyl content, not phenolic hydroxyl content.
Kraft lignin generally needs substantial treatment, such as oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction, to reach target polyurethane properties.

limitations: Most performance evidence is from laboratory foam studies, and the rigid-foam study does not provide a kraft-only pass rate in its summary.
Reported outcomes differ by lignin type and foam application; the flexible-foam study did not measure the sulfur odor it identifies as a potential drawback.
The review's TRL rating applies broadly to polyurethane uses and does not establish readiness for kraft-lignin foam specifically; another review was available only as an abstract.
The supplied feedstock profile is fictional, lacks measured molecular weight and phenolic hydroxyl content, and notes that the mill has no fractionation or chemical-modification equipment or dryer.
missing_information: The evidence does not identify named polyurethane buyers, commercial lignin-polyurethane sales, current prices, addressable volumes, contract terms, or regional demand.
It does not show whether this fictional moist filter cake meets polyurethane customer specifications or quantify the cost and practicality of the required treatment and drying.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence documents research formulations and a broad readiness assessment, but provides no documented commercial sales, named buyers, or specific market demand for lignin-based polyurethane products.

supported_claims.EV-CM-01#1: Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) specifications for lignin as a carbon fiber precursor (Baker et al. 2005) set lignin content at 99%, ash below 0.1%, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and full removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#3: Softwood lignin gives high carbon yields (55% or more) but is not readily melt-spinnable without a plasticizing agent; hardwood lignin is the reverse, with slightly lower yield (50-55%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#1: The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#2: Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#1: Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#2: Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#1: Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#2: The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#1: A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R1: Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R2: Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R3: Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R4: Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R5: Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R1: Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R2: Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.

applications.statement: Lignin is studied as a precursor for carbon fiber; the evidence discusses softwood lignin's carbon yield and melt-spinning challenges, as well as a project that advanced lignin precursor-fiber production in an industrially relevant environment.
Kraft lignin has been studied as a precursor for hard carbon for sodium-ion battery use.
Lignin can be converted to activated carbon, including lignin described as too impure for other uses.
A company announced a pilot line for lignin-based anode material for lithium-ion batteries.

target_customers.statement: Battery manufacturers and carmakers are named as parties involved in qualification of lignin-based anode materials.

competing_materials.statement: PAN-based carbon fiber is used as a cost comparator in the GreenLight project evidence.
Anthracite is listed as a hard-carbon feedstock comparator for sodium-ion battery materials.

qualification_requirements.statement: The cited ORNL carbon-fiber-precursor specifications include lignin content greater than 99%, ash below 0.1% by weight, residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm, volatile material below 5% at 250 °C, and removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
The kraft lignin examined for carbon fiber required purification, and softwood lignin requires a plasticizing agent for melt-spinning.
Battery-material qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, according to a company source.

limitations: Carbon-fiber precursor specifications are stringent, are cited secondhand, and do not apply to hard carbon or activated carbon; the cited carbon-fiber study used a non-kraft lignin source.
The carbon-fiber project reports modeled costs and project results rather than independent commercial operating data; its TRL applies to precursor fiber production, not the full production chain.
Hard-carbon evidence is a review of other studies, while activated-carbon evidence is a laboratory study using zinc chloride activation.
The lithium-ion anode pilot information is company investor material with forward-looking statements, and later project status was not verified.
The supplied feedstock profile is fictional and lacks measured sodium content; it is moist filter cake, and the profile notes the mill lacks a dryer and fractionation equipment.
missing_information: The evidence does not establish current commercial sales, named buyers, purchase prices, contract terms, or regional demand for these lignin-derived carbon products.
It does not provide hard-carbon or activated-carbon qualification standards or show whether this fictional stream meets any product-specific buyer specifications.
It does not quantify the cost or feasibility of drying and purification for this stream, or establish whether its ash and other contaminants meet carbon-fiber precursor specifications.

market_evidence.rationale: There is evidence of industrially relevant precursor-fiber development and an announced anode-material pilot line, but not documented commercial sales to established buyers. The pilot and development evidence supports the rubric's trial/pilot level.

processing_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin needs activation or depolymerization before use in phenol-formaldehyde resin; the cited process example uses a two-step process and depolymerized lignin, but its molecular-weight range is process-specific rather than a delivered-feedstock specification.
If a buyer requires dry powder, the mill would need drying equipment or a drying service; the stream is currently moist filter cake and shipping it wet increases shipped mass.
The pathway has no numeric feedstock-compatibility score: the deterministic check found no numeric evidence requirements for this pathway.
Diverting lignin to this use would require changing its current internal boiler-fuel use, and the mill has no fractionation or chemical-modification equipment.

technical_maturity.statement: The cited source reports TRL 8 for biobased phenolic-resin production generally, not specifically for this kraft-lignin stream or a mill-specific process.

adoption_barriers.statement: The pathway requires pretreatment and buyer qualification; although a supplier reports industrial proof and plywood bonding performance, the evidence does not establish named buyers, commercial sales, or fit with this fictional stream.
The stream's wet filter-cake form and lack of an on-site dryer may add handling or drying needs, while diversion also displaces its current boiler-fuel use.

current-use boiler-fuel value or opportunity cost

drying and pretreatment costs and logistics
assumptions: The economics tool used fictional scenario assumptions: wet feedstock mass of 36,000, 40,000, and 43,000 t/yr; moisture of 40%, 35%, and 30%; and availability fractions of 40%, 50%, and 60% for conservative, base, and optimistic scenarios, respectively.

The tool calculated dry mass of 21,600, 26,000, and 30,100 t/yr and usable dry feedstock of 8,640, 13,000, and 18,060 t/yr across the conservative, base, and optimistic scenarios; product output, revenue, variable costs, gross contribution, and contribution per tonne were not calculated.
All supplied feedstock values are fictional illustrative assumptions rather than mill measurements; scenario ranges should not be treated as verified operating data.
Gross contribution, if it could be calculated, would exclude capital costs, fixed costs, and the feedstock's value in its current use.
uncertainties: No TRL specifically for kraft-lignin PF resin production at this mill is established; the cited TRL is for biobased phenolic resins generally.
The feedstock's molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, and sodium content are missing, and the fictional profile's moisture and other properties require mill-specific verification.
No product yield, price, or variable-cost inputs are available, so scenario economics cannot establish commercial returns.
The cost and practical route for drying and activation or depolymerization, product qualification, buyer interest, and the value of current boiler use are unknown.

commercialization_feasibility.rationale: A technically established resin route and supplier-reported industrial plywood performance give a plausible commercialization path, but this mill lacks modification and drying assets, must displace boiler use, and would need significant investment or a capable partner and customer qualification.

feedstock_compatibility.rationale: The evidence library has no numeric requirements for this pathway to check against.

technical_readiness.rationale: TRL 8 maps to 5. Stated in EV-PF-01#3.

indicative_economics.rationale: Gross contribution per tonne could not be calculated. Missing inputs: product yield, product price, variable costs.

report.summary: Carbon materials is the only pathway that clears the scoring engine's completeness threshold, so it is ranked first among eligible pathways, with an attractiveness estimate of 2.19. This is a provisional ranking, not a finding that it is superior to phenolic resins: resins show a higher but unranked estimate (3.73) and remain insufficient-data because key criteria are unassessed. Polyurethanes are likewise insufficient-data. Prioritize mill-specific feedstock testing, buyer specifications, actual-stream trials, and route economics before committing to a pathway.

documented_facts.statement: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
In cited studies, kraft lignin replaced up to about 20% of polyol after oxypropylation, up to 50% when depolymerized and oxypropylated, and up to 100% when liquefied in a bio-based polyol.
Two of the three foams that failed were made with kraft lignin; they failed the compressive strength and/or closed-cell content requirements.

Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.

Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) specifications for lignin as a carbon fiber precursor (Baker et al. 2005) set lignin content at 99%, ash below 0.1%, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and full removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
Softwood lignin gives high carbon yields (55% or more) but is not readily melt-spinnable without a plasticizing agent; hardwood lignin is the reverse, with slightly lower yield (50-55%).
The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.

The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
A 2018 report cited by the IEA estimates the technology readiness level (TRL) for producing biobased phenolic resins at 8.
Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
